content: 1. Extrapyramidal symptoms and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) are potential adverse effects of metoclopramide. These conditions require close monitoring and caution during therapy. 2. Metoclopramide reduces bromocriptine levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination should be avoided if possible, but if used, close monitoring is essential. 3. The combination of metoclopramide and bupivacaine implants may increase the levels of either drug. Local anesthetics can elevate the risk of methemoglobinemia when used with other drugs that also cause this condition. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 4. Metoclopramide decreases cabergoline levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs and is contraindicated. 5. Chlorpromazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 6. Metoclopramide and citalopram both elevate serotonin levels, leading to an increased risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 7. Metoclopramide and clobazam may increase sedation or respiratory depression. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 8. Clozapine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 9. Metoclopramide increases cyclosporine levels by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 10. Metoclopramide and desvenlafaxine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 11. Deutetrabenazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of parkinsonism, NMS, and akathisia. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 12. Metoclopramide decreases digoxin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 13. Metoclopramide reduces dopamine levels through inhibition of gastrointestinal absorption and pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs and is contraindicated. 14. Droperidol and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 15. Metoclopramide and duloxetine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 16. Metoclopramide and escitalopram both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 17. Metoclopramide increases the effects of ethanol by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic synergy. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Increased central nervous system (CNS) depression may occur. 18. Metoclopramide and fluoxetine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 19. Fluphenazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 20. Metoclopramide and fluvoxamine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 21. Metoclopramide decreases fosfomycin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. 22. Metoclopramide and givinostat both prolong the QTc interval. If coadministered, obtain ECGs at initiation, during concomitant use, and as clinically indicated. Therapy should be withheld if the QTc interval exceeds 500 ms or if there is a change from baseline greater than 60 ms. 23. Haloperidol and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 24. Iloperidone and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 25. Metoclopramide decreases levodopa levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination should be avoided if possible, but if used, close monitoring is essential. 26. Metoclopramide decreases the effects of inhaled levodopa through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid coadministration of dopamine D2 receptor antagonists with inhaled levodopa. 27. Metoclopramide and levomilnacipran both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 28. Metoclopramide decreases lisuride levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs and is contraindicated. 29. Loxapine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 30. Metoclopramide increases the toxicity of lurasidone through antidopaminergic effects, including extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. This combination is contraindicated. 31. Metoclopramide increases the effects of meperidine by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic synergy. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Increased CNS depression may occur. 32. Metoclopramide decreases methylopa levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption and through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs and is contraindicated. 33. Metoclopramide and midazolam intranasal may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 34. Metoclopramide and milnacipran both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 35. Metoclopramide decreases nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. 36. Olanzapine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 37. Oxybutynin decreases the effects of metoclopramide through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This interaction may antagonize the prokinetic effects of metoclopramide. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 38. Paliperidone and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 39. Metoclopramide and paroxetine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 40. Perphenazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 41. Pimozide and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 42. Metoclopramide decreases posaconazole levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 43. Metoclopramide decreases pramipexole levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. 44. Prochlorperazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 45. Promethazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 46. Quetiapine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 47. Metoclopramide increases the levels or effects of red yeast rice by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction may increase creatine kinase levels and the risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 48. Risperidone and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 49. Rivastigmine and metoclopramide may increase each other's toxicity through antidopaminergic effects, including extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 50. Metoclopramide decreases ropinirole levels through pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. 51. Metoclopramide decreases the effects of safinamide through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Dopamine antagonists may reduce safinamide effects and exacerbate Parkinson's disease symptoms. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 52. Metoclopramide and sertraline both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 53. Metoclopramide and tetrabenazine both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 54. Thioridazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 55. Thiothixene and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 56. Trifluoperazine and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 57. Metoclopramide and venlafaxine both elevate serotonin levels, increasing the risk of serotonin syndrome, NMS, dystonia, or other extrapyramidal reactions. This combination should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug. 58. Metoclopramide increases the levels of vilazodone by affecting hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase vilazodone plasma levels by 50%, necessitating a reduction in the daily dose to 20 mg. Avoid or use an alternative drug. 59. Ziprasidone and metoclopramide both enhance antidopaminergic effects, increasing the risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and NMS. Caution and close monitoring are required. 60. Metoclopramide may cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), a potentially fatal condition. It should be used with caution in patients with a history of mental illness, epilepsy, or Parkinson's disease, as well as in those with hypertension, congestive heart failure, renal impairment, or cirrhosis.
